detail: supported

Parallel tree-construction algorithms enable the run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, primarily to accommodate dynamic changes in the transfer function [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that parallel tree-construction algorithms enable run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, primarily to accommodate dynamic changes in the transfer function. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 2.3.1 that 'several parallel tree-construction algorithms have been proposed to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, e.g., as a result of changes to the transfer function used.' This directly confirms every fact mentioned in the claim.
supported
The primary motivation is to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures due to changes in the transfer function [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the primary motivation is to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures due to changes in the transfer function. Source [S1] explicitly states that 'several parallel tree-construction algorithms have been proposed to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, e.g., as a result of changes to the transfer function used'. The evidence directly confirms the purpose and the specific trigger (changes in transfer function) mentioned in the claim.
supported

This approach distinguishes itself from static acceleration structures by allowing the hierarchy to be rebuilt on the GPU at interactive frame rates, ensuring that the skipping logic remains consistent with the current visual parameters [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that parallel tree-construction algorithms support 'run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping' due to changes like the transfer function. It further cites Zellmann et al. [ZHL19] showing their algorithm allows constructing an acceleration structure 'on the GPU at interactive frame rates'. This directly supports the claim that the approach allows hierarchy rebuilding on the GPU at interactive frame rates to handle changes in visual parameters (like transfer functions).
supported

The parallel nature of the construction allows for the rapid regeneration of the tree, which is necessary when the transfer function changes, as this alters which regions are considered empty versus occupied [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that parallel tree-construction algorithms support 'run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, e.g., as a result of changes to the transfer function used.' This directly supports the claim that the parallel nature allows for rapid regeneration (run-time re-construction) when the transfer function changes, which affects empty-space skipping (regions considered empty vs. occupied).
supported
The technique emerged in recent years to address the limitations of static acceleration structures in dynamic volume rendering scenarios [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique emerged in recent years to address limitations of static acceleration structures in dynamic volume rendering scenarios. The evidence explicitly states that 'In recent years, several parallel tree-construction algorithms have been proposed to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, e.g., as a result of changes to the transfer function used.' Run-time re-construction in response to changes (like transfer function updates) directly addresses the limitations of static structures in dynamic scenarios. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
This adaptation uses the boundaries of non-empty bricks as the bounding geometry for the nodes [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the adaptation uses the boundaries of non-empty bricks as the bounding geometry for the nodes [S1, unofficial]. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Zellmann et al. [ZHL19] propose an adaptation of a linear bounding volume hierarchy (LBVH) construction algorithm for triangle geometry to sparse volumetric data by using the boundaries of non-empty bricks as bounding geometry.' This directly supports the claim.
supported

Key contributions include work by Zellmann et al. [ZHL19], who proposed the LBVH adaptation for sparse data, and subsequent works by ZSL18, ZML19, FW20, DK19, DK20, and ZSL21, which further explored parallel tree construction for this purpose [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that Zellmann et al. [ZHL19] proposed an adaptation of LBVH for sparse volumetric data. It also lists ZSL18, ZML19, FW20, DK19, DK20, and ZSL21 as works that proposed parallel tree-construction algorithms to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping. This aligns perfectly with the claim.
